prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

I swallowed the sweet thing in a dream. I woke up heavy. I said, what’s the matter with you. I said, stop seeing what’s the matter with me. I ran to/from only moving one frantic eye. Something snitched. Then back to the argument. It is more acceptable to steal from the ether. When you said, we take matters into our own hands. I didn’t start the day with a ritual. Again. Twenty days and counting! I said, I was supposed to address my wrongs to you. The sweetgrass still in its plastic. Keep it there for its poetry? Then the driftwood resting on my father’s ashes. Well, you said, ecstasy from a fluted throat. Ha. As if there were presence enough in me to notice, before this. I said, I’m less angry now that you don’t exist. Then the aha moment announced. Whistling nothing like wind through fistulae. That happens here. Left to my own devices, I said. As if language were a refuge. As though the sound of walls.

With only one wild eye in motion, I fled toward and away at once. Someone tattled. And then we returned to the quarrel. Taking from the void is easier to forgive. That's when you announced, we handle things ourselves. I hadn't begun the morning with a ritual. Once more. Twenty days now, and the count goes on! I remarked, I was meant to confess my faults to you. The sweetgrass sits untouched inside its plastic. Should I leave it wrapped for the beauty of it? And then there's the driftwood laid over my father's remains. Well, you replied, rapture pouring from a flute-like throat. Ha. As though I ever held enough awareness to catch it, until now. I confessed, my anger has faded since you stopped existing. And then came the great revelation. A whistle that resembled nothing like wind moving through hollow passages. Such things occur in this place. Abandoned to myself, I said. As if words could shelter me. As if the sound that walls make.
outputs.L3:
# Awakening

I wake from the dream already weighted, as though sleep itself had pressed something into my chest that I cannot now dislodge. Before my eyes have fully opened, I am mid-argument—caught in the tense, circling exchange with a presence I cannot name and cannot silence. There is no beginning to this quarrel and no visible other; only the sensation of having been arguing for a long time, of having lost the thread of who started it and why.

The argument is old, and its subject is familiar. It concerns wrongdoing—mine, I think, though the guilt is diffuse enough to belong to no one in particular. Twenty days have passed. Twenty days of rituals left unperformed, of amends I promised myself I would make and did not, of the small ceremonies that were meant to close something and instead have been left gaping. I have counted the days without meaning to. They accumulate like a debt I keep refusing to acknowledge.

The evidence sits around me in ordinary objects. The sweetgrass remains in its wrapping, unopened, the braid I bought with such intention now only another thing I have failed to use. On my father's ashes rests a piece of driftwood—placed there once as a gesture toward meaning, and then abandoned, as though grief could be delegated to an object and left to do its work alone. These things are not neglected exactly. They are stalled. They wait for a version of me who was supposed to arrive and never did.

And yet, this morning, something has shifted. I notice—with a strangeness I cannot fully account for—that I am less angry than I was. The relief is real, though its source unsettles me: I am calmer because the presence I have been addressing no longer exists. There is no one, now, on the other side of the argument. Perhaps there never was. The absence, which should feel like loss, arrives instead as a kind of quiet.

I reach for language to steady myself, the way I always have, and find it will not hold. The words come, but they are hollow—less a shelter than a sound, the flat report of a fist against a wall. I had believed that naming a thing could comfort it, could contain it. But language, this morning, offers only its own echo: the noise of enclosure mistaken for the warmth of home.
outputs.L4:
**On the Failure of Language as a Refuge**

I.

You ask me where I put the ashes.
There is no you. There is no asking.
Still, the question arrives like weather—
a low front moving through the kitchen
where I have not lit the stove in weeks.

The ritual was simple once:
water, salt, the folded cloth,
a name spoken into the steam.
Now the bowl sits empty on the sill,
collecting the small deaths of flies.

II.

In the dream my father is a jar.
In the dream I am the hand that will not close.
He says nothing, being ash,
being the gray arithmetic of what a body
subtracts itself into.

*Are you listening,* I say to the absence.
The absence has better things to do.
It is busy being everywhere I look—
in the chair, the coat, the particular
angle of afternoon against the wall.

III.

Here is what I did wrong.
Here is the ledger, here the sum,
and here my hands, unequal to the counting.

I wanted words to be a house.
I wanted to walk inside a sentence
and shut the door against the cold.
But every room I built with speaking
opened onto the same white field
where the snow keeps its own accounting
and forgives nothing, forgets nothing,
falls.

IV.

*Say it,* the not-you insists.

I open my mouth.
What comes out is the sound
of a spoon against an empty jar,
the small percussion of a ritual
I have abandoned and cannot leave.

The ashes will not answer.
The dream dissolves at its own edges.
And I stand between the said and the unsaid—
present, absent, guilty, grieving—
holding what I cannot hold,
which is the shape of him,
which is the shape of me,
which is the shape of the word
I keep almost, almost speaking.

I'll write a text incorporating your keywords: "Something," "Then," and "When."

---

**When Something Changes**

There comes a moment in everyone's life when something shifts. It might be small at first—a passing thought, an unexpected feeling, or a quiet realization. **Something** stirs inside us, though we can't always name what it is.

**When** we least expect it, life presents us with turning points. Perhaps you're walking down a familiar street, and suddenly something catches your eye. Or maybe you're sitting alone, and a memory surfaces that changes how you see everything.

**Then** comes the choice. Once we notice that something has changed, we must decide what to do next. Do we ignore it and continue as before? Or do we embrace the shift and follow where it leads?

I remember when I first understood this. **Something** happened that I couldn't explain—a chance meeting, a book I stumbled upon, a conversation that lingered. **Then**, slowly, my perspective began to expand. **When** I looked back later, I realized that single moment had set everything in motion.

The truth is, life is full of these connections. First, **something** happens. **Then**, we respond. And **when** we look at the bigger picture, we see how each moment builds upon the last, creating the story of who we are.

---

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an experimental prose poem about addiction recovery, spiritual struggle, and grief, using fragmented interior dialogue and abrupt shifts between the concrete and abstract.
counterfactuals.output:
# What the Body Keeps

---

Morning again and the light does its usual violence against the blinds. I count them. Slats. Seven, eight—the number doesn't matter, the counting matters, the counting is a rope and I am—

*hand me the coffee.* No. *hand me the*—

There was a God here once. I keep his coat on the hook by the door in case he comes back for it, in case the weather turns.

---

Ninety days. The chip in my pocket like a communion I keep swallowing and regurgitating, cheap alloy, holy anyway, holy because I decided, because deciding is the only prayer that answers back.

You died in March. Or I died. Someone did the dying and someone stayed to do the dishes.

---

The abstract will not hold water. I have tried to carry *grace* in my two hands to the sink and it runs, it runs, it—

concrete: the faucet drips. The washcloth. The blue cup with the chip in the rim, the same word *chip* doing double duty, ninety days and a broken cup, everything I own is nicked at the edges where the mouth goes.

---

*Are you well?* asks the man at the meeting.

I am a house with the wiring pulled out. I am *fine.* These are the same sentence in different weather.

---

Grief is not a stage. Grief is a room you were always standing in, you just turned the lights on. Now you see the furniture. Now you see the coat on the hook. Now you see

that no one is coming for it.

---

God, if. God, comma, the whole prayer collapsing into punctuation, into the held breath before the word that will not—

I wanted the drink last night the way I want the phone to ring with your voice on the other end. Which is to say: I wanted the impossible dressed as the ordinary. I wanted the small brown lie of *just this once.*

---

Here is the concrete: I did not drink.

Here is the abstract: something in me knelt.

I don't know the name of what knelt. I don't know if it was faith or just the body remembering how to fold, how to make itself smaller than its wanting.

---

Seven, eight. The slats. The light.

Somewhere the coat is getting older on its hook. Somewhere you are exactly as dead as yesterday, no more, and I find this—God help me—*a mercy.* That you do not die again each morning. That grief, at least, holds still while everything else keeps

running, running, the faucet, the days, the cheap chip warming in my closed and stubborn hand.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a stream-of-consciousness piece where the speaker argues with an absent or nonexistent second person, weaving in imagery of sweetgrass, driftwood, a father's ashes, and unfinished rituals.
counterfactuals.output:
You said the fire would hold. You said—no, I'm putting words in your mouth again, that's the thing about you, you're not here to correct me so I get to invent every stupid thing you never said, and isn't that convenient, isn't that just like me, weaving you out of sweetgrass and my own resentment, braiding you the way Nana braided the long green blades, three strands, over and under, keep it tight or it frays, she'd say, keep it tight—

but I never kept anything tight, did I, and you'd agree if you were here, you'd nod that infuriating nod.

The driftwood I dragged up from the tideline is still stacked by the door, silver-gray, salt-cracked, bones of some tree that drowned somewhere and came back gray as him, gray as the tin can I still haven't opened because opening it means it's real, means you were right that I'd wait too long, that I'd let the season turn, that the water would be too cold to wade into and scatter what's left of him properly, the way he wanted, the way I promised, and a promise is just sweetgrass too, isn't it, green until it isn't, fragrant until it dries and holds its shape but crumbles when you press—

Don't. Don't say it. I know what you'd say.

You'd say I keep him on the shelf because I keep everyone on shelves, you and him and the version of me that was going to finish things, that was going to light the sweetgrass and let the smoke go where smoke goes and walk the driftwood into the surf and say the words, the actual words, not this, not this circling, this arguing with an empty chair, this braiding and unbraiding the same green rope—

and the thing is you're not even real anymore, are you, you're just the shape my mouth makes when it wants to lose an argument, when it wants someone to have been right so I don't have to be the only one who failed him.

The ash. The ash won't stay ash forever. It wants the water. Everything unfinished wants finishing, that's the cruelty, the sweetgrass wants the flame, the driftwood wants the tide that made it, he wants the going-out, and I stand here in the doorway arguing with you, you who never said the fire would hold, you who never said anything, because there was never any you—

just me, and the can, and the green braid drying on the sill, and the gray wood waiting, and the cold coming, and the words I could say right now.

I could say them right now.

I could.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a surreal, disjointed monologue that meditates on failed self-improvement ("twenty days and counting"), language as false refuge, and the tension between presence and absence.
counterfactuals.output:
Twenty Days and Counting

Twenty days and counting, or maybe counting is the thing I've been building instead of the self I promised. You should see the blueprints. Beautiful. Uninhabitable.

I said I would become someone by now. The someone is late. The someone keeps texting from a train that doesn't stop here.

*

Here is the discipline: wake, water, the word for water, the word for waking. I collect the words like a man salting an empty field, expecting bread. Language was supposed to be the house. Turns out it's the brochure of a house. Turns out I've been living in the description of shelter and wondering why my hands are cold.

*

Twenty days. Of what? The counting outlived the thing counted. This happens. A widow keeping the anniversary of a marriage that was mostly waiting.

*

I improve. Watch: I am improving right now, aren't I, the sentence has better posture. But the man behind the sentence is slumped. There's a gap between the said and the sayer and I keep falling into it, and I keep narrating the fall so nicely you'd think I meant to jump.

*

Presence was assigned as homework. Be here. I read the instructions so carefully I left. To describe the room is to step out of it and turn around to look. Every "I am here" is a postcard, which means: not here, here is where the postcard isn't.

*

Somewhere I put down a self and forgot which drawer. Twenty days I've been opening drawers. The drawers are full of drawer-words. Handle, hinge, the dark where socks go missing. Nothing wearing my name.

*

Maybe the failure is the honest part. The resolution was a costume. The relapse, at least, was skin. I keep clean for a stretch and the cleanliness feels like a very tidy absence, a swept room no one lives in, and then I break it just to hear a footstep, even if the footstep is mine leaving.

*

Language, old liar, old friend — you promised if I named the ache precisely enough it would hold still to be cured. But naming is a net and the ache is water and I am standing here holding a very fine, very empty net, saying *look how I've caught the shape of it.*

*

Twenty-one, soon. Or zero. The number resets when I'm not looking, the way the self does. I meant to be finished. Instead I'm a sentence that keeps not ending, hoping the period is a door and not just
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a contemporary poem in dense, elliptical style that blends confession and dream logic, touching on shame, wrongs to be addressed, and the futility of ritual.
counterfactuals.output:
**Penance, Unwitnessed**

I keep a small animal of the wrong I did
under the tongue. It grows a second mouth.
Nights, I wash the same doorstep twice—
the water remembers nothing, that is its mercy,
that is its refusal. Somewhere a phone rings
in a house I sold to sleep.

I confess: I let the name go cold in my hands
like a coin passed to no one.
The dream arrives wearing my father's coat
but the pockets are full of my daughters' teeth.
What is owed accrues its own weather.
I stand in it without an umbrella of any use.

They told me kneel, so I knelt.
They told me count, so I counted the light
peeling off the wall like a confession
nobody asked for. The candle does its little theater.
The ash writes *later, later* on the sill.

I was the one at the party who broke the glass
and blamed the floor. I have been the floor since.
Forgiveness, if it comes, arrives as a stranger
who won't take off her shoes, who tracks
the outside in and calls it evidence.

Every ritual is a bucket with a lit match at the bottom.
I lower it anyway. I keep lowering.
The well answers in my own voice, delayed,
saying the thing I meant to say to you
before the door, before the water,
before the animal learned my other name.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a fragmented lyric essay or prose poem exploring dissociation, spiritual bypassing, and grief, mixing sardonic asides ("Ha") with striking sensory images.
counterfactuals.output:
# On the Practice of Leaving My Body While Remaining in the Kitchen

*

They tell me to breathe into it. As if grief were a paper bag. As if I could inflate the absence until it held its own shape and stayed, obedient, on the counter beside the unwashed cup.

*

Here is the cup. Here is the ring of coffee it left, a brown planet, orbiting nothing. I have been staring at it for an hour or a year. Ha. Time is a flat circle and also a stain.

*

*Everything happens for a reason,* she said, and I watched the words leave her mouth like moths, powder-soft, aiming for the light of my face. I did not swat them. I have learned to let the moths land. To nod. To become the porch light. To buzz.

*

Dissociation is not floating. Everyone gets this wrong. It is not ascension, not the soul unspooling toward some ceiling of white. It is more like watching your own hands from the bottom of a swimming pool. They are up there. They are doing the dishes. Good hands. Loyal hands. You will meet them again someday, when the water lets you.

*

*

I have a friend who calls suffering *an illusion.* He says this from a very comfortable chair. He has not, to my knowledge, ever been the chair. Ha. I would like to be the chair. Something built to hold weight without pretending the weight is not there.

*

The morning you died the light did something ordinary. It came in. It struck the spoon. The spoon did not care. This is the part no one prepares you for: how the objects continue. How the salt keeps its saltness. How the world, that great dumb animal, keeps grazing.

*

I tried to *transcend* it. I lit the candle. I said the vowel. I held the crystal until it grew warm and useless in my palm, a stone pretending to be an answer.

And still: the smell of your coat in the closet. And still: your handwriting on the calendar, planning a March you would not use.

*

Spiritual bypassing is a beautiful bridge over a river you were supposed to drown in a little. Just a little. Just enough to know the temperature of the thing.

*

Here is what I actually believe:

That the body keeps the score and also loses the game.
That *let go* is advice from people who have never had their fingers pried open.
That the sob I swallowed at your service is still in there, calcifying, a pearl I did not want, grown around a grief I could not spit out.

*

Ha. Pearl. Listen to me. Making jewelry.

*

Some nights I come back into myself all at once, like a hand shoved into a wet glove. The kitchen resolves. The cup. The stain. The moths asleep against the window. And the grief is right where I left it, patient as a dog, having never once believed I was gone.

*

Breathe into it, they say.

Fine. Here. I am breathing.

Not into the paper bag. Not into the light.

Into the raw red room of it. Into the cup, the coat, the March.

Into the water where my hands are waiting.

Into you, into you, into the ordinary unbearable *still.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
